## Trigger

When a supervised pass hits a defect the harness itself causes, I want the pass to land every child with no human intervention from that cause, so I can reach the throughput and reliability the design targets.

## Context

Owner retro 2026-08-23 and the 2026-08-26 session: the factory is slower per unit than a bare agent, half by design and half by measured waste. - A supervised pass over this epic lands every child with no human intervention caused by a harness defect.
- A committed, clean lane is landed by the supervisor with zero agent dispatches (basicly-pjaudy).
- A behind worktree commits while a sibling record closes on main (basicly-h8dxhy).
- A `--tier` override dispatch carries measured usage and the grant stays delegable (basicly-6y0tg5).
- A landing records a per-stage timing breakdown (basicly-tjhjmk).

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `.scripts/check_release_notes.py`

## Context

Measured 2026-09-04 while the ship checkpoint for `basicly-qwqd35` was approved by hand, after
the `basicly-k6tpep` L3 grant reported `token_budget spent (104485469/100000000 tokens under
this grant; 191034258 lifetime)` and returned every checkpoint to a human.

`basicly loop run <id> --confirm <code>` refused four separately issued codes in a row, each
seconds after issue, with `checkpoint ship: REFUSED - invalid or expired confirm code`.

## Steps to Reproduce

With a record at phase `verify`, `advance ALLOWED`, and a grant that has declined the ship
checkpoint:

1. `uv run basicly loop run <id> --root <root> --runner manual` prints a code and stores it.
   Verified equal: printed `6a96a6d8`, and
   `.basicly/usage/checkpoint-confirms.json` held `{'code': '6a96a6d8'}`.
2. `uv run basicly loop run <id> --root <root> --runner manual --confirm 6a96a6d8` refuses.
3. Read the store again. It now holds a different code, `9256fa79`.

## Cause

`loop run` resolves the phase boundary before it consumes the relayed code. The advance step
hits the same ship checkpoint with `confirm=None`, so `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded`
takes the `if confirm is None` branch at `src/basicly/policy.py:1402` and calls
`_issue_confirm_code` at `:1408`, which overwrites the store entry keyed
`<id>:ship` (`policy.py:1288-1299`). The later `_consume_confirm_code` at `:1413` then
compares the caller's code against the code the same invocation just wrote, and rejects at
`:1417`.

The two steps share one key and run in the wrong order, so the relayed code is always stale
by the time it is read.

## Why it was not seen before

The bug needs a grant that declines. With a live grant the advance delegates the checkpoint
and no code is ever issued. `basicly-mfavrh` shipped through `loop run` earlier the same
session for exactly that reason.

## The path that works

`uv run basicly policy checkpoint <id> ship --approve` then the same command with
`--confirm <code>` (`src/basicly/cli.py:2784`) reaches the guard with no advance in front of
it. Printed and stored codes matched, and the approval was recorded:
`checkpoint ship: APPROVED (basicly-qwqd35)`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When a caller passes `--confirm` to `loop run`, then the invocation consumes that code
  without issuing a new one for the same checkpoint key.
- When the grant has declined a checkpoint and a code is relayed to `loop run`, then the
  checkpoint is approved.
- A regression test drives `loop run --confirm` on a record whose grant has declined, and
  fails if the store entry changes during the invocation.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

## Context

The owner states the ordering rule as "does the next state consume the previous state result".
That is a true data dependency, and it is Dagster asset-edge semantics. The shipped default rule
is different: `src/basicly/decompose.py:303` `serializes(a, b)` returns True when any glob in one
child declared write scope can match a common path with any glob in the other. It never asks what
either child produces or reads. `group_children` (`decompose.py:394`) takes the transitive closure
with union-find and `chain_predecessors` (`:431`) turns each group into a linear chain. The
literature name for ordering imposed without data flow is the GNU make order-only prerequisite.

So the owner rule orders on what flows and the code default orders on what collides. Both are
legitimate and both are already built.

## The defect

`depends_on` is a mandatory plan field (`src/basicly/plan_gate.py:77` `PLAN_FIELDS`) and the plan
gate own docstring gives the reason in the owner terms: before it existed "the only ordering
signal was scope overlap, which cannot express B needs A decision between two children that touch
no common file" (`plan_gate.py:16-19`).

At `src/basicly/decompose.py:2042-2049` the declared `depends_on` targets and the computed chain
predecessor are unioned, deduplicated and written with the same call, `dep add <child> <dep> -t
blocks`. Nothing records which rule drew a given edge. The live population holds 418 `blocks`

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-04: "do you have any suggestions how to prevent writting code against the
eplicitly stated rules, which will 100% bounce of the CI gates, rather than doing the current
loop: write code, write tests, try to commit, it bounces off."

Classified every gate refusal in that session. The expensive class was not rule violations: it
was the two size ratchets, 8 of 13 refusals. Those are not knowable from prose - the rule says
a gate exists, it cannot say that `supervise.py` has 456 tokens of headroom.

## The rule, the tool and the skill all already exist

- `.scripts/headroom.py` reports both ratchets' remaining room for a module. Its own docstring:
  "this is the read that lets a change be sized *before* it is written, which is the only point
  at which the information is cheap."
- `.claude/skills/python/SKILL.md:73` gives the command, and adds "a file with under ~200 tokens
  left wants the extraction decided now, not after the gate refuses."
- The skill is projected and available.

It was skipped anyway. `headroom.py`'s docstring records the same failure **three times in one
session on 2026-08-14** (basicly-co64), "every time by an agent who had measured tokens and not
prose". 2026-09-04 added three more. Six occurrences, all after the rule was written down.

So the guidance layer is not missing. It is advisory, and it has lost this argument six times.
`hooks.yaml` already states the remedy for exactly this shape, for `unsplit-loop-guard`: "The
always-on rule was in context and was violated anyway... Guidance that must bind becomes a hook."

## Design, with the vendor fact established rather than recalled

Verified against code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md on 2026-09-04: a PreToolUse hook's exit-0
stdout and stderr reach the debug log only and **never** the model. The one non-blocking outcome
that reaches the model is the JSON form with `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision = "allow"`
and `additionalContext`, capped at 10,000 characters.

So the hook allows every call and injects the figures. It does not block, which matters: blocking
to inform would be intrusive and would need a per-session escape hatch.

It fires only where `headroom.is_tight` already says an ordinary unit's edit would cross a bound.
Those thresholds are reused, not reinvented: `TIGHT_TOKENS = 615` and `TIGHT_POINTS = 1.0`,
measured over 44 rebaseline records.

Measured cost: 1.13s per invocation, three runs, on the `uv run --no-project` interpreter hooks
are launched with. `headroom.py` runs clean under it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When an Edit or Write targets a tracked `.py` module that `headroom.is_tight` calls tight,
  then the hook allows the call and the module's remaining tokens and prose points are in the
  model's context before the write.
- When the module has room, then the hook is silent.
- When anything fails - a malformed payload, an unreadable baseline - then the call is allowed.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/headroom-guard.py`
- `.basicly/core/hooks/hooks.yaml`
- `tests/test_headroom_guard.py`

## Context

The size ratchets are a **shared, unreserved, whole-tree budget**. Two lanes can each measure
headroom correctly, each pass their own gates, and whichever lands second bounces - because the
first spent the room in between. Neither graph models that contention, so the dependency graph
calls the lanes independent and they are not.

This is the failure the graph research names as false parallelism: nodes declared independent
that contend on a resource. See basicly-hnnmk9.9 for the inventory and basicly-zq9i2m.3 for the
file-scope half of the same gap.

## Measured, 2026-09-04, not hypothetical

`basicly-85cadb` measured its headroom correctly when it was written, and wrote the numbers into
its own `basicly.d` fragment: "`merge.py` had **0** tokens of module-size headroom, `checkout.py`
**15**, `supervise.py` **456** with **0.0** points of comment-density headroom, and
`tests/test_supervise.py` **488**."

The same fragment then declared: "`supervise.py` +296 fits inside its 456 and is not declared."

That lane sat unlanded. `basicly-ncday7` and `basicly-tjhjmk` then landed into the same two
modules and spent the room. When 85cadb was finally rebased its deltas were all stale and three
modules refused it: `merge.py` +62, `supervise.py` +297, `tests/test_supervise.py` +409. The
fragment's own sentence predicted the exact failure, and being right did not help, because the
measurement had no reservation behind it.

`merge.py` now reads `18746/18746 tokens (0 left)`. The next edit to it bounces, and nothing
tells the next lane that until it tries.

## What a reservation would do

A lane declares `## Scope` globs already, and `decompose` already compiles those into `blocks`
edges. The missing step is that a lane's declared scope should also **claim** the headroom of the
modules it names, at dispatch, so that:

- `loop preflight` refuses or serialises a second lane whose scope claims headroom already held.
- The claim is released when the lane lands or is killed, like the worktree binding.
- A lane rebasing onto a base that moved re-reads its claim rather than its stale measurement.

## Open questions a design must answer

- Where the claim lives. The worktree session record and the `basicly.d` fragment are both
  candidates; the fragment is committed and the session record is not.
- What is claimed. Whole-module headroom is coarse and would serialise more than necessary; the
  lane's own forecast delta is finer but is exactly the number lanes get wrong.
- Whether a stale claim is refused or merely reported. `contend:` is advisory today and was
  ignored - see basicly-hnnmk9.9, where 162 of 184 scope violations landed anyway.
- Whether this belongs to the ratchets or to the scheduler. Putting it in the ratchets makes
  every consumer repo pay for it; putting it in `supervise` keeps it to supervised passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- When two ready lanes declare scopes whose modules have insufficient combined headroom, then
  `loop preflight` names the pair before the pass starts.
- When a lane lands, then the headroom it claimed is released.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

## Context

`basicly-fiow1sr` (start a ready record from the board) is blocked on a capability the CLI does not have: **no verb starts one ready leaf record detached.**

Measured 2026-09-06:

- `basicly loop run --help` lists `--work-type --children --mode --confirm --root --runner --autonomy --tier`. There is no `--detach`, and the command is synchronous. `board_actions.TIMEOUT_S` is 300s against a lane that runs twenty minutes.
- `basicly loop supervise` is detachable but fans out over parent-child children. A ready leaf has none, so `loop preflight` on a task reports `lanes: 0 dispatchable now, 0 open child(ren)`.

The previous lane on `basicly-fiow1sr` built a board button whose argv was `('loop','supervise',issue,'--max-passes','1','--detach')`. It does nothing, for both reasons above, and its tests passed because they asserted the argv's shape rather than that the argv starts anything.

## The mechanism already exists

`src/basicly/cli.py:3853-3968` holds the whole detached-launch machinery: `_detach_isolation`, `_detach_argv`, `_detach_log`, `_spawn_detached`, `_detach_supervisor`. It is generic apart from one line - `_detach_argv` hardcodes `["loop", "supervise", args.issue]` - and one hand-written forwarding table, `SUPERVISE_FORWARDED_FLAGS`, pinned to the parser by `test_every_supervise_flag_reaches_the_detached_process`.

So this is a verb-aware `_detach_argv`, a second forwarded-flag table for `loop run`, and a second pinning test. The comment above `SUPERVISE_FORWARDED_FLAGS` already names the failure mode a missing table entry produces: the launching process accepts the flag and the process that does the work silently never applies it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN an operator runs `basicly loop run <id> --detach`, THE COMMAND SHALL spawn the same invocation without `--detach` in its own session, print the child pid and the log path, and return at once.
- WHERE a flag the `loop run` parser accepts is not forwarded to the detached child, A TEST SHALL fail, in the way `test_every_supervise_flag_reaches_the_detached_process` already does for supervise.
- WHEN the detached child writes output, IT SHALL append to a per-launch file under the detached-log directory, so a second launch inside the same second appends its refusal rather than truncating the first launch's log.
- WHEN `--detach` is combined with `--confirm`, THE COMMAND SHALL refuse, because a one-time confirm code relayed into a process the operator cannot watch defeats the challenge it answers.

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli_loop.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-09-06: *"lanes should not be killed if they are doing work. lanes must be inspected to determine if they hang, and conditions to kill them must be fulfilled. for example a timeout which we set is a poor condition on its own, because an agent can sometime work for hours on a task."*

**The engine already agrees with that, in writing.** `runner.DispatchBounds` says of the wall clock: *"it is the one signal that carries no information about whether work is happening"*, and `runner.StallWatchdog` is documented as *"A flag, not a kill - and deliberately the earliest of the three bounds, so a human learns about a wedge while it is still theirs to intervene in... A slow-but-working run is never cut short here."*

The defect is that none of it reaches a lane started with `basicly loop run`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `basicly loop run <id> --work-type task` on any record.
2. Read what bounds the dispatch it starts.

Measured 2026-09-06:

```
$ rg -n "StallWatchdog\(" src/basicly
src/basicly/supervise.py:2670

$ rg -n "DispatchBounds\(" src/basicly
src/basicly/supervise.py:2688

$ rg -n "runner_timeout|bounds|watchdog" src/basicly/loop.py
loop.py:891    timeout=config.runner_timeout,
loop.py:911    timeout=config.runner_timeout,
loop.py:1138   timeout=config.runner_timeout,
```

Both informed bounds are constructed in exactly one file, and it is not the one the single-lane path uses. `loop.py` passes the wall clock and nothing else.

Expected: the same three bounds, in the same order, whichever verb started the lane.

## Not hidden - stated, three times, and never closed

`loop.py` already documents its own gap:

* `loop.py:188` - *"the spend gate, the watchdog and the stream meter that only exist there"*
* `loop.py:524` - *"names the session as its grant root but has no watchdog or stream"*
* `loop.py:684` - *"watchdog or stream meter of its own"*

So this is a known asymmetry carried as a comment rather than as a record. It is the same shape as `basicly-kqh9dj8`, where lane *visibility* was keyed on the supervisor and a `loop run` lane was invisible: a capability built for the multi-lane path, absent on the single-lane one, with the difference written down and never gated.

## What this costs, measured today

Every lane driven this session used `loop run`. Each therefore ran with the poor condition alone and no stall flag. Three of them died, and the cause each time was the *host* killing the shell they were children of - which is a fourth failure mode none of the three bounds covers, and which the operator could only diagnose by reading a git worktree by hand.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN `basicly loop run` dispatches an agent, THAT DISPATCH SHALL carry the same `StallWatchdog` and `DispatchBounds` a supervised dispatch carries, so the bound that stops a lane is the one that read whether work was happening.
- WHERE a lane is quiet but its event stream, its commits or its worktree dirtiness has changed, IT SHALL NOT be stopped: the fingerprint is proof of life and restarts the clock.
- WHEN the stall bound is reached, THE ENGINE SHALL flag it for a human and SHALL NOT terminate, keeping `stall_after` below `quiet_after` as the supervised path already orders them.
- THE WALL CLOCK SHALL remain the backstop and SHALL NOT be the first bound reached on any path.
- A TEST SHALL assert the bounds a `loop run` dispatch is given equal the bounds a supervised dispatch is given, so the two paths cannot drift again.
- WHERE a dispatch dies because its parent process was killed rather than because a bound fired, THE RECORD SHALL say so, so an operator is not left inferring it from a worktree.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_loop_dispatch_bounds.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: start a lane with `loop run`, watch it idle past `stall_after`, and read the flag raised for a human while the lane is still alive - then let a working lane run past the same bound untouched.

payload.description:
## Context

Session 2026-08-14, `basicly-ejdm.2`. Nine unit tests over hand-built transcript turns all passed
against a pairing rule that was **wrong on every real transcript**. The demonstration caught it,
not the suite.

The rule paired a turn's tokens against the immediately preceding line. A real claude transcript
forwards the tool result as a `user` event carrying no usage, which sits between the call and the
turn that pays for the answer:

```text
assistant  tokens= 26234 tools=[Agent]   <- the call
user       tokens=     0 tools=[]        <- the forwarded result, no usage
assistant  tokens=     0 tools=[]
assistant  tokens= 26635 tools=[]        <- the turn that pays for the answer
```

So the rule reported a real captured lane as **100% unattributed** - a confident figure measuring
nothing. Every hand-built fixture had an assistant turn adjacent to its predecessor, because that
is the shape a person writes when they are thinking about the rule rather than the format.

## Why the existing guidance did not catch it

`test-discipline` covers isolation, order-independence and asserting on observable behaviour. All
nine tests satisfied every one of those and were still blind, because the defect was in the
**shape of the input**, not in the shape of the test.

The repo already had the evidence: `tests/test_runner_subagent_stream.py` holds a stream captured
from a live Claude Code 2.1.226 dispatch, with a comment saying every field is verbatim from that
capture. Driving it took one scratch script.

## Proposed change, for a human to apply

Add one rule to `test-discipline`: **where a live capture of the format exists in the tree, at
least one test must drive it.** A hand-built fixture encodes what the author believes the format
is, and the interesting defects are in the difference between that and what the format does.

The related rule this repo already learned from the other direction - "a dependency's error text
must be observed, not composed" (an invented fixture made a retry path dead code through two
fixes) - is the same finding for error strings. This generalises it to formats.

D25 forbids an agent amending the catalog, so this is filed rather than applied.

When a session ends on a user correction and a self-caught false claim, I want the cause written into the always-on guidance rather than into a summary, so I can stop the next session repeating it.

Finding 1, user-corrected. The sharding design put both the writer identity and the compaction in src/basicly/merge.py. Finding 2, self-caught late. SPEC.md section 4.0 was written in the same commit that shipped sharding and asserted 'The engine's landing calls the same function'. No such call existed. docs-claims passed because it catches an invented command and not a claim about a call, and compaction was run by hand three times before the gap was seen.

Not filed as findings, recorded so the branch not taken is on the record. The seam violation caught by test_gate_source and the two faulty instruments (git stash -u restoring a deleted .gitattributes, and a .git size accumulated across benchmark rounds) were all caught by controls that already exist and fired. They need no new control.

## Acceptance Criteria

- core-rules carries a bullet requiring a change under .basicly/core/kit/ to name where a consumer with no engine gets the capability.
- quality-gate carries a bullet naming a design-document sentence about a call as a claim rather than a plan.

A third finding, surfaced by this record's own commit being refused. Sharding left three readers blind because they spelled the glob as a string literal rather than reading the kit constant, so the sweep of log_paths callers that found the fold, fsck, staleness and the write-verification missed them entirely. Two of the three were already known second spellings and were fixed during the sharding work; the other three were not, and one of them - scrub_ledger - is the machine-path scrubber, so a shard carrying an absolute path would have been committed.

No new rule proposed. The repository already says to sweep the type rather than the word, and a string literal is exactly the population a type sweep cannot see. What was missing was applying it: grep the literal as well as the symbol before calling a rename complete. ## The defect

`basicly tracker show <id>` and `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py show` both return the kit fold shape and render **no edges at all**. Neither a `dependencies` nor a `dependents` key appears. So no command-line surface answers what a record blocks, what blocks it, or what its children are, one record at a time.

The engine itself has the answer. `src/basicly/tracker.py:155` `owned_record` returns `br show --json`'s shape, and `_rendered` at line 191 fills **both** directions. Its own docstring at line 202 records why the inverse direction is load-bearing: rendering only the outgoing half left `supervise.derive_session` deriving an empty session from a root whose children were all in the ledger (basicly-vkh0.29).

## Measured 2026-08-18

Same record, `basicly-vkh0.42`, three readers:

```text
basicly tracker show          keys: comments fields max_seq record status tombstoned totals
kit cli.py show               keys: comments fields max_seq record status tombstoned totals
tracker.owned_record          keys: comments dependencies dependents description id
                                    issue_type priority status title
                              dependencies: 1    dependents: 12
```

Positive control: the internal reader returns 12 dependents on that record and 1023 `edge` events exist in the ledger, so the fold has the material and a zero from the CLI is the CLI's zero, not the store's.

## Why it is priority 1

1. **An agent orients through the CLI.** The work-tracker skill points every reader at `basicly tracker show <id>` and describes the folded record as carrying exactly the seven keys above. An agent asking what a record depends on has no command that answers, and the skill does not say so.
2. **It is on the dashboard's critical path.** basicly-rn0o renders the backlog and its dependencies. A snapshot producer built over this surface would emit a graph with no edges.
3. **Two read surfaces disagree in shape.** `owned_record` and the CLI fold are separate renderings of one store. That is the drift `owned_record`'s own docstring says the kit loaders exist to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

Given a record with at least one incoming and one outgoing edge, when `basicly tracker show <id>` runs, then the output carries both directions, each edge naming its type and the other record's status.
Given a record with no edges, then both keys are present and empty, so absence is distinguishable from a surface that never renders them.
Given the kit CLI's own `show` on a repository that copied only the kit, then it answers the same question in the same shape.
Given the two readers, when the same record is read through each, then a test asserts the edge sets are equal, so the shapes cannot drift apart again.
Demonstrated by: uv run basicly tracker show basicly-vkh0.42 printing 12 parent-child dependents, against a positive control record printing none

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_cli.py`

Research spike (not implementation). Curated statements from Microsoft AI Foundry engineers building production agents describe the layers a production agent harness needs. basicly is our custom harness built ON TOP of code agents (Claude Code / Codex / Copilot) that already provide some of these layers. Goal: test basicly's design/architecture/engineering against each principle, mapping — for every dimension — (a) what the underlying code agent already provides, (b) what basicly currently does, (c) the gap, (d) concrete improvements basicly should own. File follow-up implementation beads for the accepted gaps.

Dimensions (one child task each): identity & audit trail; guardrails; observability & fleet governance; harness-as-first-class / model swappability & inference layer; agent runtime boundary; agentic context/retrieval layer; rubric-based evaluation.

Source framing to preserve: "The harness matters as much as the model" — runtime, tools, context retrieval, identity, guardrails, evaluators, deployment pipeline; models are swappable and each has different properties the harness must adjust to. "Identity bounds what an agent is allowed to reach; guardrails bound what flows through it once it acts."

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each child produces a written gap analysis (agent-provides / basicly-does / gap / recommended improvements) committed to docs or tracker comments; prioritized implementation beads filed for accepted gaps; a short synthesis rolls the seven dimensions into a basicly harness-maturity view.
